AN ENTRY IS A LAST RESORT AND NEEDS EVIDENCE. The first question is always whether the
name resolves once the right apt component is enabled -- p7zip-rar needed multiverse,
not an alias. Only a name that cannot be installed at all belongs here, and 'why' must
record what was checked rather than what was assumed.
A VIRTUAL PACKAGE FAILS IN TWO OPPOSITE WAYS AND BOTH ARE HERE. With TWO providers apt
refuses to choose and the build dies loudly (netcat). With ONE it silently installs the
provider, the build succeeds, and only a gate that iterates the DECLARED names notices
that dpkg knows the package under a different one (upx). The second is the dangerous
shape: without the gate it would never have surfaced at all.

why: On noble `netcat` is a pure virtual package with TWO providers -- netcat-openbsd and
netcat-traditional -- so apt refuses to choose and fails the whole transaction with
'Package netcat has no installation candidate'. Measured on a real debootstrapped
noble rootfs, not inferred: it took down the first end-to-end build at stage 2.
netcat-openbsd is the provider Ubuntu itself prefers -- Priority: important, in main,
against netcat-traditional at Priority: optional in universe -- and it Provides:
netcat, so the `netcat` command upstream's own Apt.Tests.ps1 expects still resolves.
`upx` is a virtual package with exactly ONE provider, upx-ucl, so apt installs it
without complaint and the build succeeds -- but dpkg then knows the package as
upx-ucl and nothing named `upx` is registered. Measured on the first image that
built end to end: the publication gate reported it missing while /usr/bin/upx
existed as an alternatives symlink and worked.
That is the opposite failure to netcat's and the more dangerous one. Nothing in the
build says anything is wrong; only iterating the DECLARED names against dpkg finds
